note: Teaching-only R5 sidecar. Quotes are verbatim passages; graph_support records the resolved edges whose content each answer states.

questions.question: scaling-strategy
questions.quote:
The available rigidity theorem is stated for the unit disk, while our
assumption concerns a disk of radius (r).  This mismatch explains the change
of scale

\[
g(w)=\frac{p(rw)}r.
\]

questions.question: schwarz-applicability-by-normalization
questions.quote:
Indeed, (\lVert w\rVert<1) implies (\lVert rw\rVert<r), so the supposition
gives (\lVert p(rw)\rVert\le r), and division by (r) gives
(\lVert g(w)\rVert\le1).  Thus scaling converts precisely the radius-(r)
bound into the unit-disk bound needed for Schwarz rigidity.

questions.question: rotation-specializes-to-identity
questions.quote:
Since
(\operatorname{dslope}(g,0,0)=g'(0)=1), this formula has slope (1), not an
undetermined rotation parameter.  The derivative identity is what makes the
divided-slope norm attain the radius ratio required by the lemma.  It does not assume
(g(0)=0); that fact is used here to remove the constant term.  Consequently
(g(w)=w) on the unit ball.

questions.question: coefficient-extensionality
questions.quote:
Applying the
coefficient function at degree (N) to the polynomial equality gives equal
degree-(N) coefficients.  The left one is (c_N), while that of (X) is zero
because (N\ge2); hence (c_N=0).

questions.question: schwarz-rigidity-connection
questions.quote:
The point (0) lies in that ball; there the divided slope is the
derivative and has norm (1).  Together with B3, these supply the equality-case
lemma's hypotheses.  The lemma returns the affine formula

\[
g(w)=g(0)+(w-0)\,\operatorname{dslope}(g,0,0)
\]

questions.question: finite-domain-coefficient-boundary
questions.quote:
That ball supplies infinitely many evaluation points, and over (\mathbb C),
agreement on an infinite set makes the two polynomials equal.
The infinitude matters: over (\mathbb F_2), the nonzero polynomial
(X^2-X) vanishes everywhere.
